title: Rare-event Evaluation & Alert Thresholds
interviewAnswer: For rare events, accuracy is usually misleading. Evaluate precision/recall, PR-AUC, recall at alert budget, expected cost and time-to-detection; choose thresholds based on operational capacity and error costs.
keyPoints: Time leakage is common in fraud/anomaly evaluation.
why: Rare-event Evaluation & Alert Thresholds appears frequently in data-science work because it connects mathematical assumptions to practical decisions, diagnostics and failure modes.
deepDive: For rare events, accuracy is usually misleading. Evaluate precision/recall, PR-AUC, recall at alert budget, expected cost and time-to-detection; choose thresholds based on operational capacity and error costs. Threshold should reflect cost/capacity. Time leakage is common in fraud/anomaly evaluation. A strong practitioner separates the modeling assumption from the estimation procedure, checks diagnostics rather than trusting a single score, and explains what would make the method inappropriate.
workedExample: If analysts can review 500 alerts/day, optimize recall among the top 500 rather than generic 0.5-threshold accuracy.
commonMistakes: Applying the method without checking its assumptions or data-generating process.
Choosing it because it is familiar rather than comparing against an appropriate baseline.
followUps: What assumptions does Rare-event Evaluation & Alert Thresholds make?
How would you validate or debug Rare-event Evaluation & Alert Thresholds in practice?
production: In production, validate assumptions on real data, monitor the quantities that can drift, and keep a simple baseline so added complexity has a measurable reason to exist.
